title: Matthew 5:33–37
context: In the Sermon’s antithesis on oaths, Jesus takes the old word against false swearing and presses speech toward simple truthfulness. The King who fulfills the Law will not let disciples prop up shaky words with heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or their own heads—and He calls for a Yes’ and No that need no sacred scaffolding, because anything more comes from evil.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic Arminian and Reformed comment on Matthew 5:33–37, in the writers’ own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Our Lord here refers to the promise made to the pure in heart of seeing God in all things, and points out a false doctrine of the scribes, which arose from their not thus seeing God. What he forbids is, the swearing at all, 1, by any creature, 2, in our ordinary conversation: both of which the scribes and Pharisees taught to be perfectly innocent.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 5:33–37)

reformed.quote: Thou shalt not perjure thyself This also is not a correction of the law, but a true interpretation of it. For God condemned in the law not only acts of perjury, but lightness in swearing, which lessens the reverence for his name. The man who perjures himself is not the only person who takes the name of God in vain, (Exodus 20:7.) He does so, who idly and contemptuously pronounces the name of God on trivial occasions, or in ordinary conversation.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 5:33–37)

verses.text: “Again you have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not make false vows, but shall perform to the Lord your vows,’
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus begins again with what the people know: do not make false vows, but keep your oaths to the Lord. The old word guards truth and vows before God.

Here the reader meets continuity with Torah and a call to listen deeper. The commandment against false oaths still stands; the question is whether disciples will stop at avoiding perjury or receive the Teacher’s fuller claim on everyday speech.
verses.reformedNotes:
“You have heard” recalls Israel’s received tradition against false swearing and for vowed performance to the Lord. Jesus does not scrap the concern for truth; He intensifies it.

The King stands over the Word He gave. What follows will not license lying but expose how oath-systems can mask a heart unwilling to simply speak true.

verses.text: but I tell you, don’t swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God;
verses.arminianNotes:
“But I tell you” widens the ban: do not take an oath at all—beginning with heaven, God’s throne. Sacred geography cannot launder unreliable speech.

The warning is earnest. Responsible discipleship refuses the habit of bolstering weak words with holy names. Jesus will not let us treat God’s throne as verbal furniture for our convenience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ’s “I tell” claims authority over the disciple’s tongue. Heaven is God’s throne—so swearing by it is never a neutral flourish; it drags the Holy into human spin.

The Law-giver exposes oath-casuistry. Grace does not need heaven as a prop; the King who sits there already owns the truth His people must speak.

verses.text: nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.
verses.arminianNotes:
Earth is His footstool; Jerusalem is the city of the great King. Lesser “holy” substitutes still belong to God—so they cannot serve as loopholes for half-true speech.

Arminian readers hear a practical summons: stop ranking oaths by sacredness to decide when truth is optional. Responsible love of neighbor means words that stand without borrowed majesty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Footstool and holy city alike fall under the great King’s claim. Graded oaths that treat some spheres as less binding are still evasion under Christ’s eye.

Creation and Zion are His. Disciples cannot invent a zone where speech is cheap. The King’s ownership of earth and city leaves no safe harbor for manipulative swearing.
verses.keyContrast: Both reject oath hierarchies that make some speech less binding. Arminians often stress responsible, grace-enabled plain truthfulness toward neighbors; Reformed readers often stress God’s total claim on creation and city, which leaves no room for casuistry.

verses.text: Neither shall you swear by your head, for you can’t make one hair white or black.
verses.arminianNotes:
Even the self is off-limits as oath-collateral. You cannot change one hair’s color—so swearing by your head pretends a sovereignty you do not have.

Grace enables humble speech. The warning is grave if we inflate ourselves with vows we cannot underwrite; the invitation is serious if we simply tell the truth. Shared confession: we are not lords of our own heads.
verses.reformedNotes:
The head-oath collapses under creaturely limit. Hair color lies outside our decree—image of how little we control even ourselves.

Pride wants a guarantee it can swear by; providence answers that we cannot whiten a single hair. Truthful speech rests not on self-sovereignty but on the God who made the head.

verses.text: But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.
verses.arminianNotes:
Simple Yes’ and No—anything more comes from evil. Discipleship of the tongue means reliability without sacred props or verbal padding.

Take the warning to heart—speak true, keep your word, drop the oath theater. Responsible response to Christ’s word means not gambling that embellished speech will somehow become honest. Shared hope: the very Lord who warns also forms a people whose ordinary Yes is enough.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Yes’ and your No’” is the King’s positive command; excess that props up speech “these is of the evil.” The issue is not mere etiquette but the source of manipulative talk.

Evil loves complexity that hides the heart. Grace frees disciples from needing oaths as crutches—Christ’s people speak under His eye, where a plain Yes already stands before the throne.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat simple Yes/No as the disciple’s norm and “be No. Whatever is more” as morally serious. Arminians underline responsible, grace-enabled integrity in speech; Reformed interpreters stress that oath-excess springs from evil and that grace frees the tongue under the King’s claim.
